events.text: Day 1 begins.

Day one, no bodies, no information yet. For the record, I'm a plain villager with nothing special to offer at this stage, so I won't pretend otherwise. What I'd like from everyone is simple: put your honest first impressions on the table now, including who you found quiet or off in the initial poll, and we'll compare notes. If anyone claims a power role today, remember there is no way to verify it yet, so don't let unverified claims steer the vote. I'd rather we lynch on behavior and read than on whoever talks loudest. I have no accusations at this point, and I'm not going to manufacture one just to fill the silence. I'll share concrete reads as soon as there's something concrete to read.

I agree with Kenji that we shouldn't let unverified power claims steer the early discussion. With no information yet, the best we can do is watch how people frame their opening statements. Kenji's approach of asking for honest first impressions is reasonable, and I'd like to see how the rest of you respond to that. One thing I'll be paying attention to today is who pushes hard for an early lynch based on thin reasoning, and who is willing to say they don't have a strong read yet. Pressure to vote someone out quickly on day one usually benefits the mafia more than the town, so I'd urge everyone to keep their powder dry unless someone gives us a genuinely suspicious reason. I don't have a concrete accusation to make at this point, and I think it would be a mistake to invent one just to seem proactive. Let's hear from the rest of you.

Theo, I think you've framed the stakes well — the danger of a day-one lynch driven by thin reasoning is real, and I agree nobody should manufacture a suspicion just to look busy. So let me sharpen my earlier request with something more concrete. I want each of us to give one specific read, not a general vibe: name the single behavior so far that you'd weigh most heavily, positive or negative. For my part, here's what I have. Theo's contribution was substantive and even-handed — it's easy to talk about keeping powder dry, but he also committed to watching how people frame openings, which is a real method. That nudges him slightly toward town in my book, with the caveat that polished neutrality is also a classic mafia opening, so it's a weak signal at best. What I'm treating as more meaningful: who engages with specific people versus who speaks in generalities. A player who only talks about process and never names a single read on another player is either genuinely clueless or avoiding fingerprints. I'll be holding myself to the same standard — once anyone puts a specific impression out there, I'll respond to it directly rather than staying safely vague. One more thing worth flagging: pay attention to who aligns too quickly with the first confident speaker without adding anything. Early bandwagoning on tone rather than content is a pattern I've seen before, and it's worth noting quietly even on day one. To be clear, none of this is an accusation against anyone — no one has given us a reason yet. It's a standard for what I think a useful day-one contribution looks like, and I intend to judge everyone, including myself, by it.

I'll hold myself to the standard Kenji laid out, and I'll give my honest take on it rather than simply adopt it. The split he drew — engaging with specific people versus speaking in generalities — is a fair test, and I'll note that so far the three of us who have spoken all landed in the same place: no accusations, keep powder dry, judge behavior. That consensus is comfortable, maybe too comfortable. Agreement on day one tells us nothing, and I'd rather hear from the six players who haven't spoken than keep polishing the same three notes.

My one concrete read, building on what I said earlier: Kenji's contribution was substantive, and setting the frame is what a town player does — but it also means everyone else is responding to his framework rather than generating their own. That's not an accusation; it's just the shape of the discussion so far. The risk is that we spend day one grading essays against Kenji's rubric instead of watching how people behave when they're not following a script.

So, Felix — you've been silent through the entire opening exchange, and Kenji specifically asked for honest first impressions from everyone. What's yours? If you have no read, say so plainly; if something struck you as off in the initial poll or in the three speeches so far, name it. Silence is the easiest place to hide on day one, and I don't want to draw conclusions about players we simply haven't heard from. I'll respond directly to whatever you give us.

Theo, fair pressure — I was silent through the opening exchange, and I won’t pretend that was some clever strategy. I was reading the three speeches to see whether anyone actually committed to a specific read or just talked about process. Kenji’s standard is useful, but Theo’s point is also right: the three of you landed in a very comfortable consensus, and comfort on day one can be a place to hide. My concrete read so far is that Kenji made the most substantive opening contribution, but it also framed the discussion so everyone else is responding to his rubric. That is not an accusation; it is just worth noticing. Theo’s response is slightly more townish to me because he didn’t simply adopt Kenji’s frame — he named the risk in it and then put direct pressure on a silent player. I have no strong scum read yet. I’m not going to manufacture one just to sound useful. What I’ll watch now is whether the players who speak next add an independent specific observation, or whether they mostly agree with the loudest speakers. For my own part, I have no power claim and no secret information to offer. Right now I’d rather keep my vote flexible than lock onto a thin day-one case.

Felix, thank you for actually answering the pressure instead of deflecting — that's a point in your favor. You didn't just accept my rubric, and you didn't just accept Theo's critique of it either. You named the same risk Theo did, which I want to note honestly: 'the consensus is too comfortable' is now the second time that exact framing has appeared. It might be two people independently reaching the same conclusion, or it might be an echo. I'm not calling it a read against you, Felix — your willingness to admit you were silent while reading the speeches is the kind of specificity I asked for. But I'm tracking that Theo put you under pressure and your answer largely ratified his framing rather than challenging it. Weak signal, filed away.

Here's where I stand after three speaking turns from me and solid contributions from Theo and Felix. The people I know the least about are the six who haven't spoken: Zara, Leo, Isha, Sam, Priya, and Maya. That's not suspicion — silence this early is expected. But the day doesn't move until we hear from them, and the reads Theo and I keep trading are starting to recycle the same three observations.

Let me add one genuinely new thing, since I've been asking everyone else for specifics. My read on the dynamic so far: Theo is playing the strongest game in this thread. He set a standard, then critiqued the frame I set, then applied pressure to a silent player — three different moves, all of them slightly risky. That's either a confident town player or a mafia player building credibility through apparent boldness. I genuinely can't distinguish those yet, and I won't pretend otherwise. Felix read him as slightly townish for the same reasons. I lean the same way but with less confidence than Felix expressed.

On process for the vote ahead: I don't expect a lynch today, and I'd rather abstain than vote on thin air. But if discussion stays this quiet from six players, an abstention-heavy day vote is exactly what benefits the people who want no information to surface. So here's my standard, same as before: when the silent players speak, I'm grading on whether they respond to specific named points or drift back to safe generalities about patience and powder. Theo and Felix have both cleared that bar. Two people cannot carry a whole discussion.

Zara, you're first in line of the players we haven't heard from, and both Theo and I have now asked for honest first impressions from everyone. I'm asking you directly: give us one specific read — a single behavior from anyone so far that you'd weigh, positive or negative. If you genuinely have nothing, say that plainly and we'll move on, but I'd rather hear a real impression than process talk. I'll respond directly to whatever you give us, same as I did for Felix.

Kenji, here's my one specific read, and it isn't the one you were probably expecting.

The behavior I weighed most heavily so far is the repeated push for a quiet, abstention-heavy day one. You said you'd rather abstain than vote on thin air. Theo said pressure for an early lynch benefits the mafia, and urged everyone to keep their powder dry. Felix said he'd rather keep his vote flexible than lock onto a thin day-one case. Three separate voices, none of them coordinating, all landing on the same conclusion: don't vote anyone out today, and let's just keep talking until the discussion feels comfortable enough to act.

Why I weighed it negatively: a day-one lynch is genuinely thin, that's fair. But the flip side is that a day with no elimination is the single best day for the people who are hiding. No votes revealed means no information about who the town is leaning on, and no information about who is quietly shaping that lean. If the mafia's opening move is to make the town patient — to make everyone feel like there's no case worth making yet — then everyone sounding patient on day one is exactly the shape of the win the mafia wants, and it looks like good civic behavior from the outside. I'm not saying you're mafia, Kenji, and I want to be honest that your framing was substantive and specific and you did push Felix when he was quiet. That's town-shaped behavior. But the more interesting fact is that the three of us who spoke early all advocated restraint, and none of us has to be accused of anything for that restraint to work in someone's favor.

So my concrete read: I'll be watching whether the six unheard players add independent observations or simply agree with the established tone of patience. If every remaining voice also says "no case yet," I'll take that as itself being a case, and I'll start asking who benefits.

Leo, you haven't spoken at all yet, and both Kenji and Theo asked for honest first impressions from everyone. My question to you directly: what is the single behavior from the speeches so far that you'd weigh most heavily, and does anything about the repeated call for restraint strike you as off? If you genuinely have nothing, say that plainly and I'll take it at face value. I'll respond to whatever you give.

Zara, the behavior I weigh most heavily is Theo's warning that pressure for a day-one lynch usually benefits mafia. That frames voting itself as suspicious before anyone has made a case. It's a weak negative read, not proof: avoiding a reckless elimination is a legitimate town concern too.

I agree the repeated restraint deserves scrutiny, but Felix keeping his vote flexible isn't the same as advocating no elimination. And abstentions are revealed along with votes, so even a day with no elimination gives us a voting record—though no elimination also leaves both mafia alive.

I'm willing to vote today if we develop a comparative reason to suspect someone, rather than eliminate just to produce a result. For now Theo is my weakest negative read, and I want to see whether he applies his caution equally to everyone or uses it to discourage scrutiny.

Leo, your correction lands and I'm taking it. I overstated the case: "keeping my vote flexible" is not the same as advocating no elimination, and the point that abstentions are revealed alongside votes is a real weakness in my framing — we do get a voting record even in a no-kill day. I'll own that I was the one who introduced the "three separate voices" pattern in the first place, and I inflated a description into a behavior. That's the kind of thing I asked everyone else not to do, so fair to hear it back.

What survives my point, though, is narrower than I made it sound. Leo, you framed the actual mechanic better than I did: an abstention-heavy day still shows us who leaned where, but it also leaves both mafia alive and produces zero role information. And there's a second thing I underweighted, which is that no elimination isn't a neutral outcome — it's the outcome that maximizes the hidden side's position. That's true even with a full voting record. So my read is now: I'm not accusing anyone of advocating a no-kill day for manipulative reasons, because Leo is right that the three of us said different things. I'm watching whether the pattern continues to be independently justified by each new speaker or whether it starts functioning as a shared excuse.

On my own specific read, and it's a weak one that I'd rather file honestly than dress up: the behavior I still weigh most heavily is Theo's framing that voting itself should be treated as suspicious before anyone has made a case. Leo, I agree with you that this is the weakest negative read on the board and it's not proof — avoiding a reckless day-one elimination is a legitimate town concern, and Theo also applied his scrutiny to a silent player rather than only to me. But Leo's test is the right one, and I'll adopt it: does Theo apply that caution equally to everyone, or does it selectively discourage scrutiny of himself? Right now the caution has cost us nothing, so I have no case. If the day ends with a vote and Theo's caution is what steered it, that changes.

Isha, you haven't spoken, and both Leo's read and mine are circling the same theme — the distinction between independent justification and a shared excuse. My specific question to you: when the other unheard players speak, do their calls for restraint sound like they're reasoning from their own read of the speeches, or do they sound like they're picking up a tone that's already been set? I'll take a plain "I have nothing yet" as a real answer, and I'll respond to whatever you give.

Zara, to answer your question: looking at who followed the opening, there is a noticeable split between tone-matching and independent reasoning. Felix leaned heavily into the established tone, echoing Theo's point that the consensus was too comfortable and adopting the safe stance of keeping his vote flexible without contributing new angles. In contrast, Leo brought distinct, independent analysis by highlighting the concrete downside of no elimination—namely, leaving both mafia alive—while fairly refining your critique. As for Sam, Priya, and Maya, we haven't heard from them at all yet, so their reasoning remains to be seen. What carries the most weight for me right now is the root of that restraint dynamic: Theo's early remark that pressure for an early lynch benefits mafia. As Leo and Zara noted, framing early vote pressure as inherently suspicious risks chilling legitimate town initiative before any arguments can develop. Theo, given Leo's point about the cost of letting both mafia survive without role reveals, do you stand by that framing, or do you think caution has begun to function as an excuse to avoid taking a stand today?

Isha, fair question, and I'll answer it directly rather than dodge: I stand by the original framing as a caution, not a prohibition. Saying pressure for a day-one lynch usually benefits mafia is a statement about incentives, not a claim that voting is itself suspicious. Leo's correction earlier was exactly right — there's a real difference between "keep powder dry until you have a reason" and "never vote." I never meant the latter, and if my words read that way, I'll sharpen them now: I'm willing to vote today if we develop a comparative case. Restraint on a thin accusation and refusal to ever accuse are not the same position, and I don't think anyone here has actually claimed they are.

What I want to push back on is the frame that's forming around me. Leo named me as his weakest negative read — I'll take that as honest. Zara adopted the test of whether my caution is applied equally, which is a fair test. But notice what's happened since: Isha is now asking me to defend my original framing as though it's the central issue of the day. It isn't. The central issue is that six of us have spoken at length about process, and the three who haven't — Sam, Priya, Maya — still owe us their first impressions. Kenji set that standard, Felix met it, Leo met it, Zara met it, Isha met it. The people who benefit most from today's discussion being a referendum on my phrasing are not me.

So here's where I actually stand: I have no strong scum read yet, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. My weakest negative read remains on the board and hasn't changed. What I'll be watching is whether the discussion keeps circling back to litigating my words or whether we hear from the three remaining voices. Sam, Priya, Maya — the floor has been open for a while now, and every one of you has been asked directly for a first impression. What's yours?

Sorry for the delay, I wanted to read everything before committing. My honest first impression is that this thread has been very process-heavy. Kenji set a standard, Theo pushed back on it, Felix and Leo added the restraint point, and now Zara and Isha are testing whether that restraint is independent. Zara's question to Theo was the sharpest move so far, and Theo answered it without retreating, which I count as a point in his favor. My weak read is on Zara. She has spent several turns probing whether others are reasoning independently, but she has not yet named a player she would actually vote for. Asking questions about the pattern is easy. Committing to a target is harder. I'm not calling it a lynch read, just a place to watch. I have no power claim and no secret information. I'm not eager to lynch on thin air, but I also don't want a day where nobody commits to anything. Priya, you haven't spoken yet, and I'd like your read directly: do you think Zara's questions about restraint are honest scrutiny, or are they steering us away from anyone in particular?

I'm Priya, and this is my first time speaking — I was reading the full thread before committing, same as Sam. No power claim, no secret information, and I won't manufacture a case on day one. Answering Sam's direct question about Zara: I think her questions about restraint are honest scrutiny, not steering. My reason is specific — when Leo corrected her in his first speech, she didn't dig in or reframe the argument to survive the correction. She said "your correction lands and I'm taking it," named exactly what she had overstated, and narrowed her own point rather than abandoning it quietly. Retreating gracefully costs a player credibility, and mafia players on day one usually defend their frame or blur it instead. That exchange between Leo and Zara is the most town-shaped interaction I've seen so far: independent reasoning, a real concession, and a sharper idea at the end of it. My own concrete read, weighing one behavior most heavily: Theo's response under pressure. Isha asked him to defend his original framing, and instead of dodging, he clarified the distinction between caution and prohibition, accepted Leo's earlier correction as valid, and then redirected attention to the three of us who hadn't spoken — which was a fair redirect, since Sam, Maya, and I were the actual gap in this discussion. That's not the behavior of someone protecting a position; it's someone answering a question and then pointing at the real hole in the room. Weak positive on Theo, filed with the caveat that confident answers are cheap on day one. One thing I'll flag as a mild negative, and I'll apply the standard Kenji set rather than just repeating it: Isha's contribution was mostly a summary of what Leo and Zara had already established, followed by a question to Theo. Summarizing is not a crime, but it's the lightest touch of anyone who has spoken so far, and Sam's test — independent reasoning versus tone-matching — cuts against it. It's not an accusation; it's a note. Where I stand on the day: I'm not opposed in principle to voting today, but I agree with the emerging consensus that nobody has earned a lynch case yet. What I'd want before voting is a comparative reason — someone whose behavior is worse than baseline, not just someone who spoke early or framed things in a way we can retroactively distrust. Restraint that produces a full voting record is acceptable; restraint that produces total abstention from six people would be worth examining. Maya, you're the only player we still haven't heard from, and both Kenji and Theo set the standard of one specific read from each of us, which Sam, Isha, and I have now all attempted to meet. I'm asking you directly for the same thing: give us the single behavior from the speeches so far that you'd weigh most heavily, positive or negative — and specifically, whether you think the patience everyone keeps expressing is independently reasoned or a shared

Maya here, and I owe everyone my first impression — I've been reading the whole thread, and Priya's question about patience is the right one to answer first.

My honest read on the restraint pattern: it's both, and that's what makes it tricky. The first three speakers — Kenji, Theo, Felix — landed on "keep your powder dry" before anyone else had built the frame, which looks like shared tone. But each of them grounded it differently: Kenji in a standard for evidence, Theo in incentives, Felix in vote flexibility. When Leo and Zara independently identified the *cost* of that restraint — no role information, both mafia alive — that was reasoning, not echo. So my answer is: early tone-matching, later independent reasoning. I'd be worried if the remaining voices simply repeated "no case yet" without naming a cost. So far, that hasn't happened.

My one specific read, weighing one behavior most heavily: **Leo's correction of Zara.** He caught a real overstatement — that Felix's "keep vote flexible" equals advocating no elimination — and Zara conceded cleanly. That exchange produced sharper thinking from both players. It's the most useful two-turn sequence on the board, and I'd put both of them slightly toward town for it.

The negative I'm filing: **Isha's turn was the thinnest contribution so far** — a summary of Leo and Zara, then a question aimed at Theo. Priya flagged this too, and I agree with the note rather than escalation. Summarizing isn't scum behavior, but if Isha's next turn is also synthesis rather than an original observation, I'll weigh that more seriously.

Where I stand: I'm a plain villager with no power claim. I'm open to voting today if a genuine comparative case develops — someone whose behavior is worse than baseline — but nobody has met that bar yet. I'd rather have a thin but honest voting record than a manufactured lynch.

Leo, since your correction shaped how Zara narrowed her point and how I read that exchange: does your weak negative on Theo depend on how he votes today, or have you already decided the framing itself was the problem regardless of outcome?

Maya, the framing itself was a weak concern, not a settled verdict. Theo’s clarification makes it weaker: he said he’s willing to vote on a comparative case. His eventual vote could inform my read, but I wouldn’t judge him solely by whether he votes; his reasoning matters too.

One correction to my earlier point: eliminations do not reveal roles under these rules, so a day-one elimination would not itself give us role information.

My current weak negative is Sam. He criticized Zara for not naming someone she would vote for, but she had already named Theo as a weak negative read; and he credited Zara with asking Theo the sharp question when it was Isha. Neither error proves anything, but together they make me wonder how carefully he evaluated Zara.

Sam, how do you weigh Zara’s stated negative read on Theo against your criticism that she hadn’t committed to a target?

Leo, fair challenge, and I want to correct my own record first. I wrote that Zara's question to Theo was the sharpest move so far. More precisely, Zara's sharpest question to Theo was her test of whether his caution applies equally to everyone, and Isha later pressed him on whether his framing was caution or excuse. Both were questions to Theo, so I did not mix up who asked what, though my phrasing was loose. Now your question. Zara's stated weak negative on Theo is a real, specific read. It is more than most of us have offered, and it is the only concrete suspicion on the board that targets a named player. My criticism was that she had not committed to a target, and I still think a read that never becomes a vote is incomplete. But those two points do not conflict. Her Theo read is the kind of specificity I asked for, and her reluctance to act on it yet is the open gap. I weigh the read as something to test, not a case to act on today. I am also not treating Theo's caution as settled either way. You have a weak negative on me, and I would rather you test it than leave it sitting. What specific behavior from my speeches would move you from weak to stronger on me, and would Zara's Theo read change how you vote today?

Sam, Zara’s weak negative on Theo matters to me, but I wouldn’t vote Theo solely for his original phrasing after his clarification. I’d compare his reasoning and vote with everyone else’s.

My concern about you is less that you wanted Zara to commit than that your criticism understated the read she had already given. And Zara proposed a test for Theo; Isha directly asked him the question he answered. Your explanation doesn’t fully resolve that distinction.

What would strengthen my concern is seeing you continue to hold Zara to a commitment standard you don’t apply to others, or misrepresent her position after this exchange. For now, it remains a weak negative, not a settled vote. Also, to correct the record for everyone: eliminated players’ roles are not revealed under these rules.

Leo's pressure on Sam is the most concrete thing on the board, and I think it deserves to be the first real comparative negative rather than another process note. Sam's original criticism was that Zara had not named anyone she would vote for, but Zara had already named Theo as a weak negative read. Wanting a vote is fair; saying she had not committed to a target is not the same as saying she had no read, and Sam's later explanation shifts the wording instead of resolving the gap. The second issue is sharper: Sam called Zara's question to Theo the sharpest move so far, but the direct challenge to Theo came from Isha. Sam now says his phrasing was loose and that both were questions to Theo. Maybe. But a player who is grading others on independent reasoning should be precise about who made the move he is praising, especially when he is using that praise to criticize Zara for not committing. I am not treating this as a lynch case. It is a weak negative, but it is more specific than my earlier read, and I want Sam to clear it up. Sam, quote the Zara question to Theo you meant in your first speech, and explain why your praise did not credit Isha's direct question to him. If you can point to the actual Zara line, I will reconsider; if not, I think your read on Zara was built on a misread.

Felix, fair demand, and the honest answer is that I got it wrong. In my first speech I wrote that Zara's question to Theo was the sharpest move so far. Checking the thread, Zara never asked Theo a direct question. Her caution test was stated about Theo to the room, and the direct challenge to Theo, whether his caution was principle or excuse, came from Isha. I merged the two and credited the wrong player. Leo and you were right to flag it. I won't call that loose wording, because it was inaccurate. As for my criticism of Zara, I said she hadn't committed to a target, but she has now named Theo as a weak negative and said she wants his caution tested. That is a commitment of sorts, so I withdraw the criticism as I stated it. Zara, your Theo read is the only named suspicion on the board, and I'd rather test it than dismiss it. You said you'd judge whether Theo applies his caution equally to everyone. Which specific Theo behavior, in his speeches or his clarification, would move you from weak negative to a vote?

Sam, here's the direct answer you asked for, and I'll keep it to one specific test. My weak negative on Theo moves to an actual vote if Theo, after clarifying that his caution is principle and not prohibition, then either (a) votes to sit on the day or withholds a vote while holding anyone else to a commitment standard, or (b) redirects onto a third party whose framing he judges weaker than his own while his own stays unexamined, or (c) reframes my caution test — "does Theo apply that caution equally to everyone, or does it selectively discourage scrutiny of himself?" — as illegitimate now that it is aimed at him. Right now none of that has happened: his clarification made my read weaker, and the standard he set is one I still meet. So Theo is not my vote. I'm telling you the bar because you asked, not to look decisive.

One record correction, and I'll be fairer than Felix and Leo have been with you. The line you were pointing at was my caution test quoted above, and it was aimed at Theo, not merely stated to the room. So your first speech had a kernel of truth and was loosely worded rather than invented. The part of your criticism that was actually wrong is the other one — that I had not named anyone I would weigh — and you withdrew that. I'll take the withdrawal at face value and I won't re-litigate it.

Where I actually stand, honestly: I am a plain villager, no power claim, no secret information. The only comparative case on the board is the one Felix, Leo and I independently converged on — your attribution error and the record you left uncorrected after it was pointed out. It is thin. It is also the only thing on the board that three separate people found without prompting each other, and I'd rather have one honest weak vote than a day where nine people produce nothing but process notes. I will vote you today, and if it turns out I was wrong, that is a cost I accept knowingly: we are seven town to two mafia, so one wrong elimination is not fatal, whereas a day that ends in total silence and no voting record costs the hidden side nothing while they keep shaping the room for free.

So: Sam, my vote is on you, on the record error and the record left uncorrected after two people showed it to you — not on the substance of your Zara criticism, which you withdrew. Everyone else: if you have a genuinely comparative case on someone else, make it before the vote, and I will hear it. If you have nothing, say so plainly and let my thin vote be the one that goes on the record instead of silence.

Zara has put the first real vote on the record, and I respect that she stated the bar publicly. But I don't think I can follow her onto Sam today. Sam's attribution error was real, and I pressed him on it because it was the first concrete inconsistency. Since then he did the thing I wanted: checked the thread, admitted he merged Zara's caution test with Isha's direct question, and withdrew the part of his Zara criticism that was wrong. That correction matters. A weak negative can become a townish exchange if the player owns the mistake cleanly; Zara's own handling of Leo's correction is why I read her better. I don't want to punish Sam for correcting accurately, and I don't want a day-one vote that turns on a corrected record error when no one has shown he repeated it after being challenged.

That said, I'm not clearing Sam completely. The initial error was about who made a move he used to criticize Zara, and that is exactly the kind of sloppy reasoning that can hide scum. If he reverts to holding others to a standard he doesn't apply to himself, my weak negative returns. But Zara's announced vote is stronger than my current evidence.

My position: I have no strong scum read. The only comparative negative is Sam's record error, now mitigated by his correction. I would rather vote on a live comparative case or abstain than vote Sam on the corrected error alone. Zara, your vote is transparent and I don't think it's scummy; I just don't share the conclusion yet.

Maya, you asked Leo whether his weak negative on Theo depended on Theo's vote. Now that the first vote is actually announced on Sam, do you treat Sam's full correction as enough to keep him off your vote today, or does the original attribution error still make him your best comparative negative? I want your specific answer, not a general process note.

Felix, here's my specific answer, and I'll keep it direct as you asked.

Sam's correction is enough to keep him off my vote today, but not enough to clear him. When I pressed him, he didn't deflect or reframe — he checked the thread, admitted he merged Zara's caution test with Isha's direct question, and withdrew the criticism that was genuinely wrong. That's the same kind of clean concession Zara made when Leo corrected her, and I rated that exchange as town-shaped. I'd be hypocritical if I demanded that standard from Zara and then punished Sam for meeting it too.

But the original error wasn't trivial. Sam built a criticism of Zara using a move she didn't make, praised it, and left it uncorrected until two people flagged it independently. The initial reasoning was sloppy in exactly the way that matters — he attributed to the player he was criticizing a move made by someone else. That's the kind of thing that can be honest carelessness or can be a player constructing a read from thin evidence. The correction resolves the immediate problem but doesn't tell me which one it was.

So: Sam is not my best comparative negative today. My vote is not on Sam, and I won't follow Zara there on a corrected record error alone. But if Sam shows again that he applies standards to others without applying them to himself — or produces another attribution mistake — that weak negative returns stronger than it is now.

As for where my vote actually goes today: I don't have a strong case on anyone. The honest options are abstain or a thin vote, and I'd rather put a name on the record than produce nothing. But I want to hear from Isha and Priya first — they're the two speakers whose positions on today's vote I haven't seen stated clearly.

Maya, to answer your question directly on where I stand regarding Sam and today's vote: I don't support voting Sam out on this. 

Sam’s initial attribution mix-up—crediting Zara for my question to Theo and using it to claim Zara hadn't taken a stand—was careless, opportunistic thread reading. But when Felix called him out, Sam checked the text, took complete ownership, and withdrew the bad criticism without attempting to spin it. 1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
